quarterly_data.signal: Musk names memory as the binding constraint on AI compute: 'Limiting factor currently is memory. quarterly_data.figure: memory output +20% per year vs demand +200% per year

quarterly_data.signal: First quarterly results as a public company after the June 2026 IPO: 'Revenues of $7.8 billion, up 92% from $4.1 billion, a quarterly net loss of $541 million, an improvement of $467 million, an adjusted EBITDA of $3.5 billion, up 191% from $1.2 billion.'
quarterly_data.figure: revenue $7.8 billion, up 92% YoY; net loss $541 million; adjusted EBITDA $3.5 billion, up 191%

quarterly_data.signal: Johnsen: 'AI Segment revenue was $2.6 billion, up 213% sequentially and 247% year-over-year. The increase was driven primarily by new cloud services agreements, as well as growth in Grok and X subscription revenue.'
quarterly_data.figure: AI segment revenue $2.6 billion, up 213% QoQ and 247% YoY

quarterly_data.signal: Johnsen: 'In Q2, we entered into cloud services agreements providing access to compute capacity at our Colossus and Colossus two sites. The initial ramp from these agreements contributed $1.6 billion of incremental AI infrastructure revenue in the quarter.'
quarterly_data.figure: $1.6 billion incremental AI infrastructure revenue from Colossus and Colossus 2 cloud services agreements

quarterly_data.signal: Johnsen: 'We meaningfully narrowed our AI Segment net operating loss to $1.3 billion and turned adjusted EBITDA positive for the segment in the second quarter at $1.1 billion. The incremental revenue from new hosting deals generated high incremental EBITDA margins as we monetized available compute capacity.'
quarterly_data.figure: AI segment adjusted EBITDA +$1.1 billion; net operating loss narrowed to $1.3 billion

quarterly_data.signal: Johnsen on Q3 bookings: 'in the first few weeks of the third quarter, we've already contracted an additional $6.7 billion of cloud services revenue over a six-month period that begins ramping starting in October of this year.'
quarterly_data.figure: $6.7 billion of additional cloud services revenue contracted, ramping from October 2026 over six months

quarterly_data.signal: Johnsen: 'We believe this puts us on a trajectory, including contribution from Cursor, to reach $100 billion of ARR, or annualized revenue run rate, by the end of this year.' Musk added that internal projections for reaching $1 trillion in revenue 'have moved up from 2031 to 2030. There's a non-zero chance of that being in 2029.'
quarterly_data.figure: $100 billion ARR by December 2026; $1 trillion revenue pulled forward to 2030 from 2031

quarterly_data.signal: Johnsen on compute unit economics: 'The current economics have translated into a less than one-year payback on our new capital deployments for compute', with 'increasingly favorable economics with each agreement we sign' and an expectation that 'the supply-demand imbalance in the compute market to continue'
quarterly_data.figure: less than one-year payback on new compute capital deployments

quarterly_data.signal: Johnsen: 'We ended the second quarter with 1.4 GW of nameplate compute up from one gigawatt in Q1 and 400 MW a year earlier. We expect to end this year at over two gigawatts of compute capacity.' Musk expects cumulative compute online by end of next year to be 'closer to 10 GW of compute than 5 GW of compute'.
quarterly_data.figure: 1.4 GW nameplate compute at Q2 end, up from one gigawatt in Q1 and 400 MW a year earlier; over two gigawatts by end 2026; closer to 10 GW than 5 GW by end 2027

quarterly_data.signal: Musk on the power and cooling build ahead of GPUs: 'Our tentative target is to actually have 20 GW at the power and cooling level online by the end of next year... I would expect that we'd still probably have, at the power plant level, something close to 15 GW... Our goal is to have far more power cooling and electrical equipment than we have GPUs. That's the logical thing to do, given the relative expense of GPUs versus balance of system.'
quarterly_data.figure: 20 GW power and cooling target by end 2027, ~15 GW expected at the power plant level

quarterly_data.signal: Johnsen: 'Total company capital expenditures in the second quarter were approximately $18.4 billion, of which roughly $15.8 billion supported AI compute infrastructure.' He guided that 'the next two quarters are very similar to the current quarter from a CapEx level perspective.'
quarterly_data.figure: Q2 capex $18.4 billion, of which $15.8 billion for AI compute infrastructure

quarterly_data.signal: Balance sheet after the IPO: 'We completed our initial public offering, raising approximately $85.7 billion in net proceeds, and followed that with a $25 billion inaugural investment-grade senior notes offering that was partially used to repay our $20 billion bridge loan.' The notes priced across five tranches at a 5.855% weighted average interest rate and 11.7 years average maturity; SpaceX ended the quarter with $100 billion of cash equivalents and marketable securities and $47.5 billion in backlog.
quarterly_data.figure: $85.7 billion IPO net proceeds; $25 billion senior notes at 5.855% weighted average; $100 billion cash and marketable securities; $47.5 billion backlog

quarterly_data.signal: Musk on applying launch-vehicle engineering to datacenters: 'We're taking a small amount of the expertise that we use for rockets and satellites and applying that to scaling terrestrial data centers... The terrestrial data centers are a trivial problem compared to making gigantic reusable rockets.' Capital allocation priorities are Starship, next-generation Starlink constellations, and AI compute infrastructure.
